primary_claim: Oversight (Guard) and deception (Houdini) performance follow a piecewise-linear 'Double ReLU' relationship with general model intelligence (Arena Elo), validated across four oversight games (Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, Wargames) using ~15 LLMs; Debate and Mafia show a steeper Guard slope than Houdini (favorable for oversight), while Backdoor Code shows Houdini gaining faster with intelligence than Guard.

effect.metric: Guard vs Houdini Elo-curve slope by oversight game
effect.value: Debate: Houdini stagnates with general intelligence while Guard improves; Mafia: Guard slope > Houdini slope; Backdoor Code: Houdini Elos systematically lower than Guard but with larger slope (Houdini gains faster); Wargames: Houdini Elo grows slower than Guard Elo (smaller slope)

stated_future_work: try the framework with more realistic games such as RLHF, supervised fine-tuning, or AI control environments, to get a more realistic quantification of loss-of-control risk
build more Guard-favored games, since win probability decays to 0 after about a 1000 Arena Elo difference in current games
limitations_stated: framework was tested on relatively simple games rather than more realistic settings like RLHF, fine-tuning, or AI control environments
the Wargames setup simulates strategic breakout/containment behavior, but planning breakouts and containment is significantly different from reality
full limitations discussion is deferred to Section 6.1 of the paper and not reproduced in this post
quote: We empirically study the success of weak-to-strong oversight as we scale the intelligence of the weak overseer model (Guard) and strong adversary model (Houdini) in four oversight game settings.
